fr:title.text: Greediness as a Predicate on Grammars?

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Greediness as a Predicate on Grammars?

fr:mainmatter.fr:p: I am not quite sure how to make everything precise, but I believe that greediness may be expressible as a predicate on tensors.

For instance, we may hope to define greediness as something like \mathsf {isGreedy} : A \otimes B \vdash \Omega
\mathsf {isGreedy}~w~(s, a , b) \colonequals \not \exists (s' , a' , b') \in (A \otimes B) w . \mathsf {stringOf}(a) < \mathsf {stringOf}(a')
Where above I mean for w, w' : \mathrm {String}, we define w < w' to mean that w is a proper prefix of w'.
In English, this attempt at a definiton would read as : a parse of A \otimes B is greedy if there is no parse of A \otimes B for the same string where the parse of A occurs over a larger substring.
This definiton cannot work exactly, as it is solely a semantic definiton. Yet it feels close to being workable internally.

A regular expression r may be unambiguous. To resolve this unambiguity one may choose to instead replace r with an unambiguous goal for parsing, or instead one may define a disambiguation strategy for r.

For instance, in Greedy regular expression matching Frisch and Cardelli alleviate the ambiguity of parsing a Kleene star by always taking the cons branch when possible. That is, when scanning over a string left-to-right with the goal of parsing a Kleene star of A and then another grammar B, we greedily parse a Kleene star of maximal length before moving on to a B.

This same greediness approach is common in parsing theory. It is also used in Regular expression containment: Coinductive axiomatization and computational interpretation and in parsing expression grammars.

Previously in Agda we had constructed equalizers in Dependent Lambek Calculus using sigma types. Further, equalizers form subobjects, which may be comprehended as maps from a type into a subobject classifier.

I believe in our formalization we want to generalize this idea to a broader class of subobjects, maybe even all of them. That is, we could define a subobject classifying grammar \Omega . Then we can internally define any predicate on a grammar g via a term p : g \vdash \Omega .

That is, forall w : \mathrm {String} we have \llbracket {\Omega }\rrbracket (w) \colonequals \mathsf {hProp}, and
\llbracket {\mathsf {subgrammar}(g)(p)}\rrbracket (w) \colonequals \mathchoice {\textstyle \sum _{{\mathopen {}\left (x : \llbracket {g}\rrbracket (w)\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \sum _{{\mathopen {}\left (x : \llbracket {g}\rrbracket (w)\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \sum _{{\mathopen {}\left (x : \llbracket {g}\rrbracket (w)\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \sum _{{\mathopen {}\left (x : \llbracket {g}\rrbracket (w)\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\llbracket {p}\rrbracket (x)}

The code for this is nearly identical to the defintion of equalizers as sigma types, and I have even built a translation of the equalizers code that is defined with this as its foundation. I have not yet tested if either implementation is preferable.

It isn't yet clear how to best expose this sort of construct syntactically. I suppose you could assume some subobject classifying grammar, but then I don't know if you can then reap the benefits of the propositions internally. That is, how do you reflect the proposition that two terms are equal in the internal language of propositions rather than the external one?

If nothing else, this code gives me a reusable interface to axiomatize smaller, sandboxed ways in which I'd like to internalize certain types of propositions (such as "two terms are equal" or "does not begin with the character c").
The hope for this code is that it let's me inductively prove the follow last soundness of Kleene star.
